title: Toolify3D
claim: Upload an STL, get a price. No human in the loop.
heroShotLabel: Hero: the quote screen with an uploaded mesh and its price
heroCaption: The customer upload screen after a mesh is parsed: dimensions, volume, material selector and the returned price.
problem: Print shops in Dhaka quote by hand over Messenger. A customer sends a file, waits a few hours for a number, and a good share of them never come back. The quote is the slowest part of a job that takes minutes to set up.
The uploaded file already contains everything the price depends on. Nobody was reading it.
built: A storefront that prices a mesh on upload, an admin dashboard for the shop, and an API between them — three services, deployed separately so the quoting path can be restarted without touching orders.

Binary STL is an 84-byte header followed by 50 bytes per triangle. Volume comes from summing the signed volume of the tetrahedron each triangle forms with the origin — a closed mesh cancels out to the true enclosed volume, so no meshing library is needed. The bounding box gives plate fit and orientation; height divided by layer height gives layer count, which is the basis for the time estimate.

Price is material cost plus machine time plus margin, and every rate in that expression lives in a table the shop edits from the dashboard. Filament goes up, they change a number — nobody deploys anything. That was the part the shop actually cared about.

Parsing runs client-side for the instant quote and again on the server when an order is placed, because the client's number is a claim, not a fact. Meshes under roughly 200k triangles resolve in under a second on Dhaka mobile data.

images.shotLabel: Upload → quote, price and time visible
images.caption: The quote screen immediately after an STL is dropped in — derived volume, price and estimated print time.
Admin order queue: each order moves through quoted, accepted, printing and collected.
The rate table — material cost per gram, machine rate per hour and margin, editable without a deploy.

change: Parsing in two places is duplicated logic waiting to drift. I'd move it entirely server-side behind a job queue and let the client show a pending state — slower to feel, simpler to trust.
The price model is also linear in volume, which means it under-quotes anything needing heavy support material. Estimating supports from overhang angle is the next real improvement.

title: MediGo
heroShotLabel: Hero: live request being matched on the map
heroCaption: A patient request in flight: symptom summary, location pin, and the doctors currently being offered the case.
problem: Getting urgent care in Dhaka means calling clinics one at a time and hoping. Directory apps list doctors by speciality, which answers the wrong question — you don't need to know who exists, you need to know who is free right now and close enough to reach.
That makes availability a live property, not a profile field.
built: I owned the request layer and the matching. A consultation request is a small state machine — open, offered, accepted, withdrawn, closed — and every transition is a server-authored event over Socket.io. The client never decides it won a race.

When a patient opens a request, the server fans it out to on-call doctors inside a starting radius, ranked by distance. The first accept wins and the server immediately withdraws the offer from everyone else, so two doctors can't both believe they took it. If nobody accepts within thirty seconds the radius widens a step and the offer goes out again.

Distances are straight-line haversine against coordinates from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim geocoder, which is accurate enough to rank candidates and free to run at competition scale. Doctors publish availability as a toggle with an implicit expiry, because the failure mode we cared about was a doctor who went home and left themselves marked on-call.
Judged 2nd of 135 teams at the Asset Skill Competition.

images.shotLabel: Patient request screen, waiting for accept
images.caption: The patient's view while a request is out — offered doctors and the current search radius.

images.shotLabel: Doctor's incoming offer with accept action
images.caption: A doctor's incoming offer, showing distance and how long the request has been open.

change: Live request state lived in server memory, which is fine for a demo and wrong for a product: restart the process mid-request and the request is gone. It belongs in the database with the socket layer as pure transport.

Fan-out also filtered a broadcast rather than using rooms per district, so the work grew with total doctors instead of nearby ones. That's a rewrite of about forty lines and it's the first thing I'd do.

title: NBA Cyber-Cell
claim: Harassment reports, triaged and tracked. National rollout.
heroCaption: The triage queue: reports ordered by severity, each showing assignee, age and current state.
problem: Reports of online harassment were arriving as Facebook messages and phone calls. There was no record of who had seen what, nothing structured enough to hand to police, and no way to tell a reporter what had happened since.
The people using it are often frightened and on a borrowed phone. That constrains the design more than any technical requirement does.
built: A submission form that needs no account, and behind it a triage queue that makes the handling visible. Reporters get a reference code; entering it later shows the current stage without exposing anything about who is working the case.

The queue is the real product. A report arrives unassigned, gets a severity, gets an owner, and every action after that appends to a log that cannot be edited — only added to. When a case is escalated, that log is the handover document, which is why nothing in it is overwritable.

I collect as little as the workflow allows. No mandatory identity, evidence uploads scoped to a case and served through short-lived signed links rather than public URLs, and admin access gated by role with the reporter's contact detail visible only to the assigned owner.
Building this after a year of security work made one thing obvious: the threat model here is not an attacker on the internet, it's a careless insider with a login.

images.caption: The submission form — no account, minimum fields, reference code issued on submit.

images.shotLabel: Case detail with append-only action log
images.caption: A case with its append-only action log — the record that travels with an escalation.

change: Append-only is enforced by the application, which means a database admin can still quietly rewrite history. Chaining each entry to a hash of the previous one would make tampering detectable instead of merely inconvenient.
The form also assumes a working connection. Someone on a weak signal loses what they typed, and for this audience that is not a minor bug — a local draft is next.

title: Sportnest
claim: Booking platform with JWTs verified against a remote JWKS endpoint.
heroShotLabel: Hero: booking flow with a slot selected
heroCaption: The booking grid: a venue's slots for one day, with held and taken slots distinguished.
problem: The default way to add auth to a booking app is to give the application server the secret it signs tokens with. Compromise the app once — an injection, a leaked environment variable, a dependency — and the attacker can mint a valid token for any account, including the owner's.
A booking platform holds money and personal schedules. That's worth designing around.
built: Signing and verification are separate concerns held by separate services. The auth service owns the private key and never exposes it; the API only ever verifies.

Public keys are published as a JWKS document, each with a key id. A token names the key that signed it in its header, and the API resolves that id against the remote key set using `jose`, cached with a TTL so verification isn't a network call per request. Rotating a key means publishing a new one and letting the old one age out — no redeploy, no shared secret to copy between services.

Authorisation is checked against the resource, not the role. A booking belongs to a user; the handler compares the token subject to the record's owner rather than trusting a role claim, because roles are what get over-granted first as an app grows.
It is a small platform and this is more machinery than it strictly needs. I built it this way because I wanted the pattern in my hands before I need it on something larger.

images.caption: Slot selection — availability resolved per venue and day before a booking is held.
A user's own bookings — every read here is scoped by the token subject, not by role.

change: Sessions currently slide forward on activity. Short-lived access tokens with rotating refresh tokens and reuse detection would let a stolen token expire on its own and reveal the theft when the old one comes back.
The key cache also has no way to be told to drop early, so an emergency rotation waits out the TTL. A push channel for invalidation is the missing piece.
